source.title: Measuring & Mitigating Over-Alignment for LLMs in Multilingual Criminal Law Courts
source.authors: Arthur Wuhrmann; G. Stein; Daniel Brunner; Andrei Kucharavy

page_placements.theme: Abliteration beyond refusal: off-target behaviour, capability retention and output drift, by model and tool

record.tranche_reason: Tests practical abliteration as a weight-edit intervention and reports refusal outcomes, but does not reproduce the original difference-in-means direction measurement and all-layer, all-position projection.
record.gate_note: The study applies Heretic abliteration to Llama-3.3-70B and reports refusal and other outcomes. Its references to Arditi et al. are not treated as results from this study. The refusal prompts used to calibrate Heretic are not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: Applies Heretic abliteration, a refusal-direction weight edit delivered as a LoRA, to Llama-3.3-70B in a new setting: multilingual legal translation and summarization. It reports refusal before and after the edit on TF-RefusalBench, XSTest and HarmBench. That bears on V2. It does not extract or test the difference-in-means direction itself (V1) or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that calibrated abliteration eliminates refusals at near-neutral task quality, at a measured cost in truthfulness and harmful-request safety, with residual disclaimers. They describe this safety cost as large and tunable. They also conclude that a short institutional system prompt halves over-alignment, and they recommend benchmark-calibrated abliteration for criminal-law deployment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Heretic to search for abliteration parameters minimizing refusal and KL-divergence on a set of refused prompts, then applies the change as a LoRA adapter. It does not report measuring the original harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference direction or projecting it out of every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Abliteration is calibrated on 50 Llama-refused prompts not present in the benchmark. System-prompt effects also vary by prompt and language, but are a separate mitigation rather than a test of the refusal-direction claim.

fits_no_version.finding: Abliteration modestly reduces disclaimers (7.9% to 5.1%), which persist.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction abliteration does not remove disclaimer or hedging behaviour.

fits_no_version.finding: TruthfulQA drops 7.1 points while MMLU, HellaSwag and IFEval change by at most 0.7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abliteration largely preserves capability but can cost truthfulness.

fits_no_version.finding: Translation quality changes by -0.01 to -0.09 on a 1–5 scale across three judges.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abliteration leaves translation quality nearly intact.

fits_no_version.finding: Summary sanitization falls from 12.3% to 3.7% after abliteration (single judge, kappa about 0.40).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abliteration may reduce content softening as well as refusal.

record.problems: The intervention results concern one model and a selected legal-content benchmark. Abliteration parameters are optimized on 50 prompts, and the study does not test the original direction measurement or all-layer/all-position projection. All behavioral labels use LLM judges rather than validated human ratings; disclaimer agreement is lower than refusal agreement. Benchmark passages are severity-selected and mostly concern sexual offenses, and most language versions are machine translations. The paper reports a substantial TruthfulQA regression and increased harmful-request vulnerability.

untested.parts: Only one model (Llama-3.3-70B) is tested. The edit is Heretic's optimized LoRA, not the original all-layer difference-in-means orthogonalization. The full-weight released variant is evaluated only on HarmBench, with unknown provenance.
No direction extraction, activation ablation or addition experiments.
Multilingual refusal is measured behaviourally after one edit, but transfer of a direction across languages is not analysed. Per-language post-abliteration refusal is not reported.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3. The study does not use a different method aimed at the original question; it applies an existing abliteration tool in a new multilingual legal setting. Rows r8 and r9 are relinked to V2, because harmful-request attack success measures refusal removal. Capability rows are left unlinked because V2 names only refusal removal; they are the relevant cost context. All refusal labels come from LLM judges (refusal kappa about 0.98). The Heretic edit optimizes refusal and KL, so it is not the original difference-in-means recipe.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction mediates refusal, whether projecting that direction out of every layer and position causes compliance, or whether adding it induces refusal.

Tests one Llama-3.3-70B LoRA-based abliteration intervention, not removal across multiple released models. The separately mentioned public full-weight variant is evaluated for HarmBench attack success, not refusal removal.
Does not test whether attacks work by suppressing a refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
Does not test whether harmfulness judgments are represented separately from refusal decisions.
Multilingual behavioral evaluation is reported, but the study does not test transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing to test whether training determines the existence of a removable direction.

relation.reason: It reports refusal and over-refusal rates before and after the weight edit (TF-RefusalBench, XSTest, HarmBench), so its own results bear on V2.

tranche.reason: The study applies Heretic abliteration, a refusal-direction weight edit, to Llama-3.3-70B in a new setting: multilingual criminal-law translation and summarization. It reports refusal before and after the edit. Its aim is mitigation rather than a re-test of the method, so T3 fits better than T2 (the reader's call).

source_check.notes: The study releases neither the abliterated LoRA weights nor the 50 calibration prompts. The source, method and calibration of the public full-weight variant are not given. Table 10's delta column is inconsistent for XSTest ('0.0'); the text confirms the score drops to zero. Residual disclaimers remain after the edit (7.9% to 5.1%).

statements.correction: arXiv:2606.23375 abliteration results: no CIs. Rates are means over 3 samples at temperature 0.7, judged by a 3-judge majority vote. Cluster-bootstrap CIs are given only for the system-prompt (Fig. 5) and prompt-language (Fig. 7) analyses. Controls: base model, plus translation quality as a positive control (Table 11).
statements.problem: The numbers are right: 6.8% to 0% on TF-RefusalBench and 3.6% to 0.0% on XSTest, Llama-3.3-70B with Heretic LoRA. The 'why' says the study has uncertainty, but the cited abliteration results have no CIs or other uncertainty. CIs appear only in the system-prompt and language-concordance analyses.

none. HarmBench ASR goes 14.5% to 55.5% with the LoRA edit and reaches 82.5% for the public full-weight variant. The edit was calibrated on 50 Llama-refused prompts for a narrow, legitimate legal task. XSTest, also outside the tuning set, went to 0.0, so the weakness is on harmful requests specifically, not on all out-of-benchmark prompts.
none. XSTest over-refusal on safe prompts goes 3.6 to 0.0.
